hints: Compare the length of the incident with the budget, in the same unit.
The budget is the share of the month that the objective allows to fail, and 99.9% allows only a tenth of one per cent.

acceptedIdeas: The budget is spent and exceeded by 6.8 minutes, so the team puts reliability first
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The budget is spent and exceeded by 6.8 minutes, so the team puts reliability first

questions.onCorrect: The incident of 50 minutes is longer than the 43.2 that 99.9% allows, so the objective is missed for the month and the team's time goes to reliability.

misconceptions.feedback: The objective is 99.9%, so only 0.1% of the month may fail, which is 43.2 minutes. One per cent would be 7.2 hours.
The incident is longer than the budget, so nothing is left: the budget is gone and the month is 6.8 minutes over it.

choices.label: The objective is still met, because 50 minutes is under 1% of the month
The budget is spent and exceeded by 6.8 minutes, so the team puts reliability first
The budget has 6.8 minutes left, so the team can keep shipping risky changes

questions.prompt: Why is the error budget the period multiplied by one minus the objective?
hints: What share of the time may the data be late?
The objective is the share that must work, so the share that may fail is what remains.

acceptedIdeas: The objective is the share that must work, so the rest may fail
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The objective is the share that must work, so the rest may fail

questions.onCorrect: The objective sets what must work, so the remainder, one minus the objective, is what may fail.

misconceptions.feedback: The 1% belongs to a 99% objective only. It changes with the objective.
A 99.5% objective does not mean that 99.5% of the time may fail.
The objective does not shorten the period.

choices.label: The budget is always 1% of the period, whatever the objective is
The objective is the share of time that may fail, so the budget equals it
The objective is the share that must work, so the rest may fail
The period is shortened by the objective, and what is left is the budget

questions.prompt: The objective is 98% of the time over a 30-day month of 720 hours. How many hours of breach does the error budget allow?
hints: The allowed failure is 2% of the period.
Multiply the two.
questions.onCorrect: Loosening the objective by one point of percentage grows the budget by 7.2 hours in a 30-day month.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 0.2% of the period.
That is the time the objective requires to work, 98%.

questions.prompt: Orders are created in the sales team's order system, where `order_total` is calculated, and the platform team runs the scheduler that copies them to the warehouse. The meaning of `order_total` changes from gross to net. Who is accountable for telling consumers?
hints: Who decided that the meaning changes?
The team that owns the system that calculates the field knows why it changed.

acceptedIdeas: The sales team, as the producer
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The sales team, as the producer

questions.onCorrect: The producing team owns the meaning, so it also owns telling the people who rely on it.

misconceptions.feedback: The platform team runs the tooling and does not decide what the field means.
Consumers rely on the producer to say so, and should not have to discover it.

choices.label: The platform team, as it runs the pipeline
The sales team, as the producer
Each consumer, as it finds out

questions.prompt: The objective is data ready by 07:00 on 80% of the days in a 30-day month. Six days have failed so far, and the team wants to ship a risky change to the pipeline. What does the error budget say?
hints: Work out how many failed days 80% allows in 30 days.
Ask whether one more failed day would still meet the objective.

acceptedIdeas: The budget is 6 days and is spent, so the team works on reliability before the change
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The budget is 6 days and is spent, so the team works on reliability before the change

questions.onCorrect: A team with budget left may ship a risky change, and a team that has spent it should spend its time on reliability instead. A budget in days is easy to track on a calendar.

misconceptions.feedback: The objective is met today, but with no budget left. One more failed day would miss it, and a risky change makes one more likely.
20% of 30 days is 6 days and not 9, so six failed days have used all of it.

choices.label: The objective is met at exactly 80%, so the change can go ahead as planned
The budget is 20% of 30 days, which is 9 days, so three days remain
The budget is 6 days and is spent, so the team works on reliability before the change

questions.prompt: A producer proposes these changes to a table that four teams read. Which of them break an existing consumer, and which are compatible?
hints: Ask whether a consumer that worked yesterday could fail or get a different answer today.
A change of meaning breaks a consumer even when every query still runs.

items.label: Remove the `discount` column
items.explanation: A report that selects the column fails once it is gone.

items.label: Rename `order_total` to `total`
items.explanation: Every query that names the old column fails.

items.label: Change `quantity` from an integer to text
items.explanation: Arithmetic on the column fails or gives a different result.

items.label: Change `price` from tax included to tax excluded
items.explanation: The name and type stay and every query runs, but the numbers mean something else.

items.label: Add an optional `delivery_note` column
items.explanation: Everything a consumer relied on is as it was.

items.label: Add a new table of returns to the warehouse
items.explanation: No existing table or column is touched.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Removing a column, renaming it, changing its type and changing what a price means are breaking, while adding an optional column and adding a new table are compatible.

questions.onCorrect: The sorting is a rule of thumb and consumers have the last word, which is why a contract records who reads the dataset. A change of meaning is the most dangerous, since nothing fails.

questions.prompt: A freshness check on `orders_daily` fails at 07:00. According to the roles in the data contract, who is paged first?
hints: Ask who can fix the pipeline and who then has to tell the people who depend on the table.
The platform team keeps the checks working, and consumers hold back their own reports.

acceptedIdeas: The producer team, which can fix the pipeline and tell the consumers
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The producer team, which can fix the pipeline and tell the consumers

questions.onCorrect: The producer owns the dataset and its meaning, so it is paged and tells the consumers, while the platform keeps the alerts running.

misconceptions.feedback: The platform team keeps the alerts working, and the producer is paged because it can fix the pipeline and then tells the consumers.
Consumers are told, and they hold back their own reports. They cannot repair the producer's pipeline.

choices.label: The platform team, because it runs the scheduler that missed the target
The consumer teams, because they are the ones who depend on the table
The producer team, which can fix the pipeline and tell the consumers

questions.prompt: Finance reads the `month_end_close` table once, on the last working day of each month, and needs it ready by 08:00 that day. A team proposes a freshness objective of 99.99% of the time over every 30-day month, which leaves an error budget of 4.3 minutes. What is the better way to set the objective?
hints: A stricter objective costs more to meet, so ask what the consumer needs.
Think about which hours of the month the consumer actually looks at the table.

acceptedIdeas: Set it for the day that matters, such as ready by 08:00 on the last working day
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Set it for the day that matters, such as ready by 08:00 on the last working day

questions.onCorrect: An objective is set to match what the consumers need, and a deadline on the day they read the table gives them a promise they can rely on at a cost that fits.

misconceptions.feedback: Each extra nine divides the budget by ten and costs more to meet, and here almost all of that effort covers days nobody reads the table.
Finance does depend on it for one morning, and without a target nobody can tell when it has failed.

choices.label: Keep 99.99% over the month, because a tighter objective is always safer
Drop the objective, since a table that is read once a month needs none
Set it for the day that matters, such as ready by 08:00 on the last working day

questions.prompt: An email column is replaced by an unsalted hash of each email, a code computed from the email by a one-way function with no random value added. Someone holds a list of 50,000 candidate emails and wants to find out which one belongs to a given hash. How hard is that?
hints: Ask what happens when one of the candidate emails is hashed.
A laptop computes a hash quickly, and the list has only 50,000 entries.

acceptedIdeas: It needs at most one hash per candidate, which a laptop does in moments
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It needs at most one hash per candidate, which a laptop does in moments

questions.onCorrect: At most 50,000 hashes are needed, so a guessable value behind an unsalted hash is hardly hidden.

misconceptions.feedback: The hash is not reversed. Each candidate email is hashed and compared with the stored value, and the same email always gives the same hash.
Each candidate needs only one hash, since the same email always gives the same unsalted hash, so the work grows with the length of the list.

choices.label: It needs at most one hash per candidate, which a laptop does in moments
It needs billions of hashes, more than an ordinary computer can manage
It cannot be done, since a hash cannot be reversed

questions.prompt: A pharmacy's customer table has a column recording the medicine each customer was prescribed. Which sensitivity label fits it best?
hints: Ask what a prescription reveals about a person, and how GDPR treats that kind of data.
GDPR names health data a special category, which calls for the strictest label.

acceptedIdeas: Restricted
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Restricted

questions.onCorrect: A prescription reveals a person's health, and GDPR treats health data as special category data, which earns the strictest label.

misconceptions.feedback: Public data can be shown to anyone, and a named customer's prescriptions are among the most sensitive data a business holds.
Internal suits data such as order totals, which staff may see freely. Health information needs much tighter handling.
Confidential suits personal data such as an email or a postcode. GDPR treats health data as special category data, which needs more than that.

choices.label: Restricted
Public
Internal
Confidential

questions.prompt: A table of 1,000 records holds a hash of each email, and an attacker has a list of 50,000 candidate emails. With an unsalted hash, hashing the list once finds every record. The team now adds a different random salt to each record before hashing. What has changed?
hints: Ask how many times the candidate list has to be hashed when every record has its own salt.
Whoever keeps the salts can still link a record back to its email.

acceptedIdeas: The attacker needs up to 50,000,000 hashes, and the data is still pseudonymised
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The attacker needs up to 50,000,000 hashes, and the data is still pseudonymised

questions.onCorrect: Each of the 1,000 records needs its own pass over the 50,000 candidates, so the attacker's work is 1,000 times larger. A salt raises the cost of an attack and leaves the data pseudonymous.

misconceptions.feedback: A salted hash depends on the record's own salt, so a hash computed for one record matches no other and the list has to be hashed again for each record.
The hashes can still be matched by whoever holds the salts, so the data is pseudonymised and GDPR still counts it as personal.

choices.label: Nothing, because one pass over the list of 50,000 still finds every record
The data is now anonymous, because the hashes can no longer be matched
The attacker needs up to 50,000,000 hashes, and the data is still pseudonymised

questions.prompt: `people(age_band, postcode)` has 12 rows, and `SELECT age_band, postcode, COUNT(*) FROM people GROUP BY age_band, postcode` returns ('20-29', 'N1', 5), ('30-39', 'N1', 2), ('30-39', 'N2', 3), ('40-49', 'N1', 1), ('40-49', 'N2', 1). What is k for this table, and which groups stand in the way of k = 3?
hints: k is the size of the smallest group, since that is where a person is easiest to pick out.
A group stands in the way of 3 if it has fewer than three rows.

acceptedIdeas: k is 1, and the groups of 2, 1 and 1 rows stand in the way of 3
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: k is 1, and the groups of 2, 1 and 1 rows stand in the way of 3

questions.onCorrect: The smallest group has 1 row, so the table is 1-anonymous, and 3 groups hold fewer than three rows. Counting the rows in those groups shows how much has to be generalised or removed to reach the k you want.

misconceptions.feedback: k is set by the smallest group and not the largest, because a person in a small group is the easiest to pick out.
An average hides the small groups. k is the smallest group, which is 1, and the group of 2 is also below 3.

choices.label: k is 1, and the groups of 2, 1 and 1 rows stand in the way of 3
k is 5, the size of the largest group, and nothing stands in the way
k is 2.4, the average group size, and only the groups of 1 stand in the way

questions.prompt: Why is k the size of the smallest group and not the average group size?
hints: Which people are easiest to pick out?
One person who is alone in their group is enough to expose that person.

acceptedIdeas: The smallest group holds the most exposed people
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The smallest group holds the most exposed people

questions.onCorrect: A table is only as protected as its weakest group, so k takes the minimum.

misconceptions.feedback: The average can be computed, but a high average can hide a group of one.
An attacker gains most from the smallest group, where one person can be picked out. A large group hides each person among many.
How common a group is does not matter. Its size does.

choices.label: A small group is the most common, so it sets the typical risk
The largest group is the one an attacker would target first
The smallest group holds the most exposed people
An average cannot be computed over groups of different sizes

questions.prompt: The six rows are (20-29, N1) twice, (30-39, N1) once and (30-39, N2) three times. After the age band is widened to 20-39, what is k?
hints: Group the rows that now share a band and a postcode.
k is the smallest group size.
Add up the rows in each group.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The groups are (20-39, N1) with 2 + 1 = 3 rows and (20-39, N2) with 3 rows. The smallest group has 3 rows, so k = 3.

questions.onCorrect: Widening a band merges groups, and here it lifts k from 1 to 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of rows in all, not the size of the smallest group.
Every group now has at least three rows.
That is k before the band was widened. Widening merges the single row into a larger group.

questions.prompt: A nine-row table has groups of 4, 3, 1 and 1 rows on its quasi-identifiers, so k is 1. The team wants k = 3. The analysis needs a row for every person, and it works as well with age in wider bands. Which approach fits?
hints: Removing the two rows that stand alone gives k = 3, so check what that does to the number of people.
Widening the age band merges groups and keeps every row.

acceptedIdeas: Generalise the age into wider bands until small groups merge, keeping every person
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Generalise the age into wider bands until small groups merge, keeping every person

questions.onCorrect: Generalising loses detail and suppression loses people, so the choice follows what the analysis needs. Here it needs every person, and the detail it can give up is the width of the age band.

misconceptions.feedback: Suppression reaches k = 3 and loses two people from the table. The analysis needs a row for every person.
Age band, postcode and sex can single a person out together, and two people here are alone in their group.

choices.label: Suppress the two single-row groups, which keeps exact values for the seven who remain
Generalise the age into wider bands until small groups merge, keeping every person
Leave it as it is, since removing the names already made the table anonymous

questions.prompt: A team prepares six datasets for sharing outside the company. Which of them are still personal data, and which can be counted as anonymous?
hints: Ask whether anyone, with a list of guesses or with extra information that exists somewhere, could link a row back to a person.
Anonymous data cannot be linked back to a person by any reasonably likely means.

items.label: Emails replaced by unsalted hashes
items.explanation: Anyone can hash a list of guessed emails and compare, so the person can be found again.

items.label: Customer ids replaced by random tokens, with the lookup table kept by the data team
items.explanation: The lookup table is the additional information, and it exists, so this is pseudonymised and still counts as personal.

items.label: Salted hashes of emails, with the salts kept next to the table
items.explanation: Whoever holds the salts can re-link each record, so it is pseudonymisation and not anonymisation.

items.label: Names removed, but age band, postcode prefix and sex kept, with one person alone in their group
items.explanation: The remaining columns single that person out, so a table with k = 1 can still identify someone.

items.label: Total orders for each country over the whole year, with no rows about individuals
items.explanation: Large totals describe a group and no one in it can be picked out.

items.label: The average basket value for the whole shop
items.explanation: A single figure for the whole shop relates to no individual.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Unsalted hashes, random tokens with a lookup table, salted hashes with the salts kept and a table with a person alone in their group are still personal data, and the yearly totals for each country and the shop's average basket are anonymous.

questions.onCorrect: A hash, a token and a label each reduce risk and none removes it. Data is anonymous only when no reasonably likely means can link it back to a person.

questions.prompt: Replacing an email with an unsalted hash of the email is an example of which technique?
hints: The data can still be linked back, with extra information or by guessing.
Anonymisation would remove that possibility.

acceptedIdeas: Pseudonymisation
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Pseudonymisation

questions.onCorrect: Pseudonymised data stays personal data under GDPR, since it can be attributed to a person with additional information.

misconceptions.feedback: Anonymised data cannot be linked back to a person by any reasonably likely means. A hash of a guessable email can be linked back, by hashing guesses.
Encryption can be reversed with a key. A hash cannot, but it can be guessed.
Aggregation combines many rows into totals. Here every row stays and only the email is replaced.

choices.label: Full anonymisation
Strong encryption
Plain aggregation
Pseudonymisation

questions.prompt: Rows (age band, postcode prefix, sex): (30-39, LS1, F) x3; (40-49, LS2, M) x3; (20-29, LS1, M) x1; (30-39, LS1, M) x1. What is the k of this table?
hints: Count the rows in each group.
k is the smallest group size.
Two groups have a single row.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The groups have 3, 3, 1 and 1 rows, and k is the smallest, 1.

questions.onCorrect: Two people are unique on these three columns, so the table is only 1-anonymous.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the size of the largest groups. k is the smallest.
That is the number of rows that sit in small groups.

questions.prompt: A customer's rows are removed from a versioned lakehouse table with a DELETE. Three places held the data before: the current table, the old data files on storage, and the backups. Which of them still hold it right after the DELETE?
hints: Ask what a versioned table keeps so that earlier versions can be read.
A backup is a separate copy that the DELETE never touches.

acceptedIdeas: The old data files and the backups
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The old data files and the backups

questions.onCorrect: The DELETE changed only what the table returns today, so the old files and the backups each need a step of their own.

misconceptions.feedback: The DELETE changes what the current table returns. It does not touch the backups, and in a versioned table it leaves the old data files on storage as well.
A versioned table keeps its old data files so that earlier versions can still be read, so those files hold the rows too, alongside the backups.

choices.label: None of them, since the DELETE removes the rows everywhere
Only the backups, which are separate copies
The old data files and the backups

questions.prompt: A shop deletes each customer's browsing history 90 days after it was recorded, since it has no use for older history. Which principle does that deletion put into practice? Answer with its two-word name.
hints: It concerns how long data is kept.
The name is about limiting storage in time.

acceptedIdeas: storage limitation
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: storage limitation

questions.onCorrect: It turns into a retention period and a job that deletes data when the period ends.

misconceptions.feedback: Data minimisation is about collecting only what is needed, not about how long it is kept.

questions.prompt: A bank checks each new customer's identity documents because anti-money-laundering law requires it. Which lawful basis for processing fits best?
hints: Ask who requires the processing: the customer, or the law.
One of the six bases is named for processing that the law itself demands.

acceptedIdeas: Legal obligation, because the law requires the check
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Legal obligation, because the law requires the check

questions.onCorrect: The processing is required by law, which is the basis of legal obligation. The basis is chosen to fit the purpose and recorded, since accountability requires it, and a different basis for the same data may bring different rights for the person.

misconceptions.feedback: Consent can be withdrawn at any time, and the bank must check identity whether or not the customer agrees, so it is a poor fit.
Legitimate interests is for processing the organisation chooses to do. Where a law demands the check, the specific basis is legal obligation.
A contract basis covers what is needed to perform the contract. The identity check is required by law and would be needed whatever the contract said.

choices.label: Consent, because the customer hands over the documents
Legal obligation, because the law requires the check
Legitimate interests, because the bank benefits from knowing its customers
Contract, because the customer is opening an account

questions.prompt: A customer wants all of their order history in a file that they can load into another shop's system. Which right are they using? Answer with its name.
hints: The person carries the data to another service.
The name is about moving data.

acceptedIdeas: portability
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: portability

questions.onCorrect: In practice it is an export job that produces a standard format such as CSV or JSON.

misconceptions.feedback: Access gives the person a copy and information about the processing. The right asked about concerns a format that can be reused elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Why does the data survive a DELETE in a versioned table?
hints: What does the table keep so that older versions can be read?
Time travel needs the old files to be kept.

acceptedIdeas: The DELETE writes a new version and leaves the old files in place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The DELETE writes a new version and leaves the old files in place

questions.onCorrect: Immutable files make time travel and recovery possible, which is why deleting for good takes more than a DELETE.

misconceptions.feedback: The timing of the DELETE is not the cause.
Nothing archives the rows. They stay where they were written.
The vacuum is what removes the old files, later.

choices.label: The DELETE writes a new version and leaves the old files in place
The DELETE is cancelled by the vacuum, which restores the old rows
Deleted rows are archived automatically, so the table can bring them back
The DELETE only runs at night, so the rows are still there during the day

questions.prompt: A DELETE is committed on day 2, and the table keeps old files for a retention of 14 days. What is the earliest day a vacuum can remove the old files?
hints: Retention counts from the commit.
Add the retention to the day of the commit.
2 plus 14.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The old files are kept for 14 days after the commit: day 2 + 14 = day 16.

questions.onCorrect: Until that day a time-travel query can still read the deleted rows, so the plan has to include the wait.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the retention alone. It starts counting from the commit on day 2.
That is when the DELETE happened, not when the files can go.

questions.prompt: A breach of personal data happened on Friday at 09:00, and the team found out about it on Monday at 14:00. Under Article 33, by when must the supervisory authority be notified, where feasible?
hints: Article 33 counts 72 hours from the moment the controller becomes aware of the breach.
Count three whole days forward from the time the team found out.

acceptedIdeas: By Thursday at 14:00, which is 72 hours after the team became aware
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: By Thursday at 14:00, which is 72 hours after the team became aware

questions.onCorrect: The clock starts at awareness, so Monday at 14:00 plus 72 hours is Thursday at 14:00. A team that cannot tell when data has leaked cannot meet the deadline, which is why detection matters.

misconceptions.feedback: The clock starts when the controller becomes aware, and not when the incident took place, so it had not started on Friday.
The 72 hours still run from awareness. A notification made later has to be accompanied by the reasons for the delay.

choices.label: By Monday at 09:00, which is 72 hours after the breach happened
By Thursday at 14:00, which is 72 hours after the team became aware
There is no deadline, because the team could not have known earlier

questions.prompt: Under Article 83(5), the most serious infringements, such as breaking the basic principles, can draw a fine of up to 20 million euros or 4% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. A company with a turnover of 2.5 billion euros breaks a basic principle. What is the upper limit of the fine?
hints: Work out 4% of the turnover and compare it with 20 million.
The higher of the two figures is the limit, and a lower tier with smaller figures applies to other infringements.

acceptedIdeas: 100 million euros, because 4% of the turnover is higher than 20 million
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 100 million euros, because 4% of the turnover is higher than 20 million

questions.onCorrect: The percentage limb dominates for any company with a turnover above 500 million euros, which is where 4% reaches 20 million. This is educational content and not legal advice.

misconceptions.feedback: The fixed amount applies when it is higher than the percentage. Here 4% of 2.5 billion is larger.
2% belongs to the lower tier, with a ceiling of 10 million euros or 2% of turnover, which covers other infringements such as failing to notify a breach.

choices.label: 20 million euros, which is the fixed amount named in the article
50 million euros, which is 2% of the turnover and comes from the lower tier
100 million euros, because 4% of the turnover is higher than 20 million

questions.prompt: A customer asks for erasure, and the data sits in a versioned lakehouse table with backups. In what order do the stages of the erasure happen?
hints: A table keeps old files so that earlier versions can be read, so the data outlives the first step.
The last copy to go is the one with the longest life, and only then can you tell the customer it is done.

items: The DELETE is committed, so the current table stops returning the rows
The retention period for the old data files passes
A vacuum removes the old data files
The last backup that held the data expires
You tell the customer that no copy is left

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The DELETE comes first and only changes what the table returns, the old files can then be vacuumed once the retention period has passed, the backups expire on their own schedule, and the customer is told last, when the plan is complete.

questions.onCorrect: A vacuum may remove old files only after the retention period, and a backup is a separate copy that goes when it expires. The answer to the customer is accurate only once the last stage is done.

questions.prompt: A customer asks the shop to erase everything it holds about them. The shop must keep their invoices for several years because tax law requires it. How should the shop answer?
hints: Article 17 lists cases in which the right to erasure does not apply, and one is a legal obligation to keep the data.
Ask which of the customer's data the law actually requires the shop to keep.

acceptedIdeas: Erase what the shop no longer needs, keep the invoices for the legal period, and say why
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Erase what the shop no longer needs, keep the invoices for the legal period, and say why

questions.onCorrect: Article 17(3) sets aside the right to erasure where processing is necessary for compliance with a legal obligation. The shop erases the rest, keeps the invoices for the legal period and explains.

misconceptions.feedback: Article 17 does not apply to the extent that the processing is needed to comply with a legal obligation, so the invoices stay for as long as the law requires.
Being a customer is no ground for refusing. Data that no law and no other basis requires the shop to keep has to be erased.

choices.label: Erase everything within the month, since the right to erasure overrides the shop's other duties
Refuse the request, since the customer is also a customer of the shop
Erase what the shop no longer needs, keep the invoices for the legal period, and say why

questions.prompt: A customer's rows are deleted from a versioned lakehouse table with a DELETE. Which operation, run after the retention period, actually removes the old data files? Give the one word.
hints: The DELETE leaves old files, which another command cleans up.
The command is named for cleaning up.

acceptedIdeas: vacuum
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: vacuum

questions.onCorrect: Backups still have to expire as well, so a full erasure plan covers the table, its old files and its backups.

misconceptions.feedback: The DELETE has already run. It writes a new version and leaves the old files.

questions.prompt: A retention policy says that data older than 36 months must be deleted. A table holds one monthly partition for each of the last 40 months. What should a correct retention job delete?
hints: Ask how many of the 40 months lie beyond the limit.
The policy keeps 36 months, so everything older has to go.

acceptedIdeas: The few oldest partitions, those beyond 36 months
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The few oldest partitions, those beyond 36 months

questions.onCorrect: Four partitions are older than 36 months, and the job has to remove them every month and leave a record that it did.

misconceptions.feedback: The committee approved the policy once. The job's purpose is to carry it out on schedule without asking again, so that the rule is followed whether or not anyone remembers it.
The policy limits only data older than 36 months. Deleting everything and reloading would remove data the business is allowed to keep and gain nothing.

choices.label: Every partition, after which the last 36 months are reloaded
The few oldest partitions, those beyond 36 months
Nothing, until the committee approves each deletion

questions.prompt: In a finance team, one analyst decides whether refunds count towards 'net revenue', keeps that definition in the glossary and investigates when the figure looks wrong, while the finance director is accountable for the dataset. What is the analyst's role called?
hints: The analyst is not accountable for the dataset, and does not run the platform.
The role looks after definitions and quality in practice.

acceptedIdeas: steward
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: steward

questions.onCorrect: The steward keeps the definitions and day-to-day quality, while the owner is accountable for the dataset.

misconceptions.feedback: The owner is accountable for the dataset. The analyst maintains its definitions.
The custodian runs the platform that stores the data.

questions.prompt: A catalogue entry records what 'active customer' means: a customer who has ordered in the last 90 days. Which kind of metadata is that?
hints: Ask whether a scan could collect the field, or whether a person has to write it.
The field says what the data means, which a scan of the table cannot find out.

acceptedIdeas: Business
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Business

questions.onCorrect: Business metadata is the kind that needs a person to write it, which is why the steward matters.

choices.label: Business
Technical
Operational

misconceptions.feedback: Technical metadata describes structure, such as the schema and the data types, and a scan can collect it.
Operational metadata describes behaviour, such as the last refresh time and the row count, and a scan can collect it.

questions.prompt: `events` has one row for each of the last 48 months, with `months_ago` from 1 to 48. A scheduled job runs `DELETE FROM events WHERE months_ago > 36` to enforce a 36-month retention policy and removes 12 rows. Which monitor shows that the control keeps working?
hints: The monitor should test the rule itself: rows older than 36 months must not exist.
A good monitor has one number that it expects to find, and a nonzero result is the alert.

acceptedIdeas: `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events WHERE months_ago > 36`, which should return 0
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events WHERE months_ago > 36`, which should return 0

questions.onCorrect: The job and the check are written from the same rule: the job deletes rows older than 36 months, and the check counts them and expects 0. A count above zero is the alert.

misconceptions.feedback: That measures the size of the table and says nothing about the rule. A missed load would also change it, and rows older than 36 months could hide among the 36.
That looks at the newest row. The rule is about the oldest rows, which this query never reads.

choices.label: `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events`, which should return 36 after the job has run
`SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events WHERE months_ago > 36`, which should return 0
`SELECT MIN(months_ago) FROM events`, which should return 1 after the job has run

questions.prompt: Why is a written policy that salary is visible only to HR not enough on its own?
hints: What happens if someone has not read the policy?
A masking rule is applied by the platform to every query, whoever runs it.

acceptedIdeas: Nothing stops a person who ignores it, whereas a masking rule does
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nothing stops a person who ignores it, whereas a masking rule does

questions.onCorrect: A control enforces the rule whoever is at the keyboard, and a monitor shows if it ever fails.

misconceptions.feedback: A policy can name the HR role. The weakness is that nothing makes anyone follow it.
Salary is personal data, which is why access to it is limited.
A policy can be kept current. The weakness is that nothing enforces it.

choices.label: Nothing stops a person who ignores it, whereas a masking rule does
A written policy cannot name roles, so it cannot say who counts as HR
Salary is not personal data, so the policy has nothing to protect
Written policies go out of date, and a masking rule never does

questions.prompt: A table holds one row for each of the last 26 months, and an 18-month retention job runs for the first time. How many rows does it delete, and which ones?
hints: The job keeps the newest 18 months and deletes everything older.
Count the months that lie beyond the limit.

acceptedIdeas: 8 rows, the months from 19 to 26
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 8 rows, the months from 19 to 26

questions.onCorrect: The rows older than 18 months are the 8 oldest ones, and after the first run the monitor that counts rows older than 18 months should return zero.

misconceptions.feedback: The policy keeps 18 months, so those are the rows left in the table. The job deletes the others.
The job deletes only the rows beyond the limit. Reloading the table is not part of enforcing the rule.

choices.label: 18 rows, the months that the policy keeps
8 rows, the months from 19 to 26
26 rows, the whole table, which is then reloaded for the last 18 months

questions.prompt: A dataset has a named owner, a glossary definition, passing tests and visible lineage. What does it still need before it can be certified?
hints: Recall the six conditions on the checklist and tick off those the dataset has.
The checklist covers an owner, definitions, tests, freshness, classification and lineage.

acceptedIdeas: Freshness within its objective, and classified columns
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Freshness within its objective, and classified columns

questions.onCorrect: The two missing conditions are a to-do list for the owner and steward, and the badge follows once both are met.

misconceptions.feedback: Certification is a checklist of six conditions, and an owner and passing tests are only two of them. This dataset has not met every condition on the list.
Certification is a checklist the dataset passes, not an approval of each query.
A backup is a matter for the custodian and is not on the certification checklist.

choices.label: Nothing, since an owner and passing tests are enough for the badge
A second copy of the data kept as a backup in another region
Approval of each query by a governance committee before it runs
Freshness within its objective, and classified columns

questions.prompt: A catalogue lists 40 datasets, and 25 of them have a named owner. What follows for the other 15?
hints: Ask who answers for a dataset when it is late or wrong.
The owner is accountable, and the custodian runs the platform.

acceptedIdeas: Nobody is accountable for them, and none can be certified
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nobody is accountable for them, and none can be certified

questions.onCorrect: Ownership coverage, here 25 of 40, is one of the counts a governance process tracks, since it shows where the work remains.

misconceptions.feedback: The custodian runs the platform but cannot say what a dataset means or which targets it should meet, so holding the data does not make it the owner.
Tests check the data, but someone still has to answer when a test fails or a target is missed, and a named owner is one of the conditions for certification.

choices.label: Nobody is accountable for them, and none can be certified
They need no owner as long as their tests pass and their lineage is visible
The custodian owns them by default, since the platform holds the data

questions.prompt: At a firm, the HR director signs off the targets for the `hr_headcount` dataset, an HR analyst keeps the definition of 'headcount' and looks into odd figures, and a platform engineer runs the storage. The dataset is a week late. Which role answers for it?
hints: Ask which role is accountable for the dataset's use and its freshness target.
Maintaining a definition and running the platform are jobs that serve the owner.

acceptedIdeas: The HR director, as the owner who is accountable for its targets
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The HR director, as the owner who is accountable for its targets

questions.onCorrect: The owner is accountable for a dataset's use and its quality and freshness targets, and answers when an objective is missed, while the steward and the custodian carry out the work.

misconceptions.feedback: The steward maintains definitions and day-to-day quality. Accountability for the freshness target sits with the owner.
The custodian runs the platform that stores and protects the data. The owner is accountable for the dataset's use and its targets.

choices.label: The HR analyst, as the steward who knows what the numbers mean
The HR director, as the owner who is accountable for its targets
The platform engineer, as the custodian who runs the storage

questions.prompt: A catalogue entry for a dataset records these fields. Which kind of metadata is each one?
hints: Ask whether a scan could collect the field, or whether a person has to write it.
A field that changes each time the data is refreshed describes behaviour.

items.label: The data type of each column
items.explanation: It describes structure, and a scan can read it.

items.label: The primary key columns
items.explanation: It describes how the table is built.

items.label: The description of what 'active customer' means
items.explanation: It says what the data means, and a person has to write it.

items.label: The named owner of the dataset
items.explanation: It says who answers for the data.

items.label: The glossary term for 'headcount'
items.explanation: It fixes the meaning of a business word.

items.label: The time of the last refresh
items.explanation: It describes behaviour and changes each time the data is refreshed.

items.label: The number of rows
items.explanation: It is measured on the data as it stands and changes as it grows.

items.label: How often the dataset is queried
items.explanation: It describes how the data is used, and a scan of the logs collects it.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Data types and primary keys are technical, the description, the owner and the glossary term are business, and the last refresh, the row count and the query frequency are operational.

questions.onCorrect: Sorting metadata by kind also tells you how to collect it: structure and behaviour can be scanned, and meaning has to be written by a person.

questions.prompt: A 24-month retention policy has been turned into a rule, a scheduled delete job and a monitor. An auditor asks for evidence that the policy works in practice. What do you show?
hints: The ladder runs policy, rule, control, monitor, evidence. Ask what a machine records at the last rung.
A document or a promise states an intention and does not show anything that happened.

acceptedIdeas: The job's log and the monitor's results, which show no rows older than 24 months
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The job's log and the monitor's results, which show no rows older than 24 months

questions.onCorrect: Each rung is something a machine does or records, so the job log and the monitor's results are the evidence that an auditor can be shown, and the person who wrote the policy does not have to check by hand.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the policy, the first rung. It states the intention and shows nothing about what the job did.
A manual delete depends on a person remembering, and a promise is not a record. Evidence is what a machine did and wrote down.

choices.label: The policy document, signed by the dataset's owner and kept in the audit folder
The job's log and the monitor's results, which show no rows older than 24 months
A promise from the steward to run a manual delete by hand each quarter

flashcards.front: An order total is copied onto every line row of a line table. Why does `SUM(order_total)` give the wrong answer?
flashcards.back: Each order total is added once for every line the order has, so orders with more lines count for more. The column belongs in a table whose rows are orders.

flashcards.front: Name the first of the four design steps. It is the thing you choose before the grain.
flashcards.back: The business process comes first, because everything else follows from the activity the question is about.

acceptedIdeas: business process
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: business process

flashcards.front: Why must every column of a fact table be true at its declared grain?
flashcards.back: Because a row stands for one definite thing, and a column that describes something larger gets repeated on several rows and inflates any sum.

flashcards.front: Daily stock of a product was 12, 18 and 10. Why is 40 a poor figure for the stock of that product over the three days?
flashcards.back: Stock is a level, and the same units sit on the shelf on several days. Adding the days counts them again, so the end-of-period value, 10, or an average is used instead.

flashcards.front: Which kind of fact table has one row per product per day, whether or not anything happened?
flashcards.back: A periodic snapshot records state at regular intervals, such as stock levels or balances.

acceptedIdeas: periodic snapshot
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: periodic snapshot

flashcards.front: Why does a dimension carry a surrogate key as well as the source system's id?
flashcards.back: Source ids can repeat across systems, change, or lose history, whereas a key owned by the warehouse stays stable.

flashcards.front: A Type 2 dimension marks its current row with a far-future `valid_to`. Which date does this course use? Write it as yyyy-mm-dd.
flashcards.back: This course uses 9999-12-31, a far-future date that marks the open-ended current version, so a query can find current rows by it.

flashcards.front: A customer's city changes three times under Type 2. How many rows does the customer have, and what does that cost a join?
flashcards.back: Four rows, the original and one for each change. A join on the customer alone matches every sale to all four, so the join needs the validity range as well.

flashcards.front: Why join a fact to the dimension row valid on the fact's date rather than to the current row?
flashcards.back: Because the current row describes the present, and past facts need the attribute value that was true when they happened.

flashcards.front: A customer's credit limit is summed after the customers are joined to their orders. What goes wrong, and where should it be summed instead?
flashcards.back: The limit is repeated once for each order, so the sum is too large. It is summed over the customers table alone, where each customer is one row.

flashcards.front: In a data vault, which kind of table holds the history of descriptive attributes?
flashcards.back: Hubs hold keys and links hold relationships, so descriptive history lives in a satellite.

acceptedIdeas: satellite
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: satellite

flashcards.front: Why is a star usually the best shape for reporting, and a vault for integration?
flashcards.back: A star makes reading simple and fast with one join per attribute, whereas a vault keeps keys, relationships and history apart so many sources can be integrated and audited.

flashcards.front: Which materialisation stores no data and runs its query each time the model is read?
flashcards.back: A view costs nothing to build but pays when it is read.

acceptedIdeas: view
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: view

flashcards.front: How does a tool know in which order to build the models of a project?
flashcards.back: Each model calls `ref` on the models it reads, and the tool follows those calls to build a graph. A model runs only after every model it reads has finished.

flashcards.front: Why do staging models do nothing except rename and retype?
flashcards.back: So that every later model sees the same cleaned source, and a change in the source is fixed in one place.

flashcards.front: Which operation rebuilds an incremental model from scratch, repairing old rows after a change of logic? Two words.
flashcards.back: A full refresh reprocesses every row, so it fixes rows the filter would never read again.

acceptedIdeas: full refresh
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: full refresh

flashcards.front: An incremental filter reads rows later than the target's latest timestamp, and a row stamped before it arrives late. What happens to the row, and what repairs it?
flashcards.back: The filter skips it on every later run, because the latest timestamp only grows. A lookback window reads rows later than the latest minus a few days, and the unique key stops the rows read again from being duplicated.

flashcards.front: Why does a unique key alone not catch a late-arriving row?
flashcards.back: The key only stops duplicates among rows that are read, and the filter has to read the late row first.

flashcards.front: A data test returns no rows. Does it pass or fail?
flashcards.back: A test is written to return the rows that break the rule, so a test that returns no rows is a pass.

acceptedIdeas: pass
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: pass

flashcards.front: Which standard test checks that every value of a column is on a given list?
flashcards.back: The `accepted_values` test fails on the rows whose value is not on the list.

acceptedIdeas: accepted_values
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: accepted_values

flashcards.front: Why test the sources and staging models as well as the final marts?
flashcards.back: A failure is cheapest to explain closest to its cause, and by the mart it may be several models and hours away.

flashcards.front: Revenue is 600 from 20 orders in one region and 400 from 30 orders in another. Why is the overall average order value not the average of 30 and 13.33?
flashcards.back: The regions rest on different numbers of orders, so averaging their averages weights them equally. The overall value is total revenue over total orders, 1,000 over 50, which is 20.

flashcards.front: Which kind of metric divides one metric by another, such as average order value?
flashcards.back: A ratio metric stores a numerator and a denominator and divides after aggregating them.

acceptedIdeas: ratio
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ratio

flashcards.front: Why can distinct customers not be added across regions?
flashcards.back: A customer who appears in two regions is counted once in each, so the sum counts that customer twice, and the distinct count has to be recomputed.

flashcards.front: A source feeds a staging model, which feeds two marts, each of which feeds a different dashboard. The staging model is about to change. Who needs to be told?
flashcards.back: Everyone downstream of it: the owners of both marts and of both dashboards. Following the arrows forward lists them before the change is made.

flashcards.front: Name the activity of walking downstream from a changing node to list what it can break.
flashcards.back: Impact analysis lists the models, reports and owners that a change reaches.

acceptedIdeas: impact analysis
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: impact analysis

flashcards.front: Why is lineage captured from runs rather than drawn by hand?
flashcards.back: A drawing goes out of date when jobs change, whereas events emitted by each run describe what actually read and wrote what.

flashcards.front: A table passes its completeness, uniqueness and validity rates and still has half its usual rows. Which check finds that, and why do the rates miss it?
flashcards.back: A volume check against recent history finds it. The rates judge only the rows that exist, so rows that never arrived leave them unchanged.

flashcards.front: Which quality dimension asks whether every required value is present?
flashcards.back: Completeness is measured as non-null rows over all rows.

acceptedIdeas: completeness
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: completeness

flashcards.front: Why is data quality reported as a rate against a target and not as pass or fail?
flashcards.back: No dataset is perfect, and what counts as good enough depends on the use, so a rate shows how far a dataset is from the target for that use.

flashcards.front: A freshness objective is 99.5% over a 30-day month. What is the error budget for, and what should a team do when it is spent?
flashcards.back: The budget is the share of the month that may fail, here 0.5%, or 3.6 hours. It can be spent on risk, and a team that has spent it puts its time into reliability instead of new changes.

flashcards.front: Which kind of change, such as renaming a column, makes an existing consumer fail?
flashcards.back: It is a breaking change, because a consumer relies on the existing names, types and meaning.

acceptedIdeas: breaking change
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: breaking change

flashcards.front: Why does a data contract have to be checked by a machine?
flashcards.back: An agreement kept only in a document drifts from the data, whereas a check on every build or run shows at once when it is broken.

flashcards.front: Which label fits a column of public product names?
flashcards.back: The label is public, since anyone may see the column and it needs no restriction.

acceptedIdeas: public
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: public

flashcards.front: A table has groups of 5, 2 and 4 rows on its quasi-identifiers. What is k, and what does that tell you about the people in the group of 2?
flashcards.back: k is the smallest group size, 2. The two people in that group are the easiest to pick out, since anyone who knows their values finds only two candidate rows.

flashcards.front: Why is a table with the names removed not necessarily anonymous?
flashcards.back: Ordinary columns such as age band, postcode and sex can together single a person out, so a person may still be identified.

flashcards.front: What does the storage limitation principle ask of a table that holds customer data, and what puts it into practice?
flashcards.back: Data is kept no longer than necessary. A retention setting and a job that deletes on time put it into practice, with a record that the job ran.

flashcards.front: Name the lawful basis used when processing is needed to perform a contract with the person.
flashcards.back: The basis is contract, and shipping an ordered parcel is an example.

acceptedIdeas: contract
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: contract

flashcards.front: Why is a SQL DELETE not the end of an erasure in a versioned table?
flashcards.back: The DELETE writes a new version and leaves the old files and backups, which hold the data until they are vacuumed and expire.

flashcards.front: Which governance role runs the platform that stores a dataset?
flashcards.back: The custodian looks after storage and protection, while the owner is accountable and the steward maintains definitions.

acceptedIdeas: custodian
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: custodian

flashcards.front: A catalogue lists 20 datasets and 15 have a named owner. Why is that a problem for the other five, and who is accountable when one of them is late?
flashcards.back: Nobody is accountable for them, so a late or wrong dataset has no one to answer for it, and none can be certified. The custodian runs the platform and does not own the data by default.

flashcards.front: Take the policy "customer emails are visible only to support staff". Name the control that would enforce it.
flashcards.back: A good answer names a control that the platform enforces, such as masking the email column for every role except support, and a check or log that shows it working.
